Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 11, verse 1:

﴿Alif-Lam-Ra.﴾ ﴿A Book﴾: meaning the Qur'an. It is the predicate of an omitted subject (khabar ibtida', i.e., "this is a Book"). ﴿Its verses have been made precise﴾: that is, perfected, so it derives from ihkam (making a thing sound and firm). ﴿Then detailed﴾: it has been said that the meaning is "explained clearly," and it has also been said that it means "divided into surahs, one surah after another." Here "thumma" (then) does not indicate sequence in time; rather, it indicates sequence in states, like your saying: "So-and-so is noble in origin, then noble in deed."

**Qur'an 11:2–3:** ﴿That you worship none but Allah.﴾ "That" (an) is explanatory (mufassira); some say it is verbal-masdariyya, in a position of an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi), or a substitute for "the verses," or it may be an independent statement, cut off from what precedes it, spoken on the tongue of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). What supports this is His saying: ﴿Indeed, I am to you a warner and a bringer of good tidings from Him.﴾ ﴿And that you seek forgiveness from your Lord and then turn to Him in repentance.﴾ That is: seek His forgiveness for what preceded of polytheism (shirk) and sins, then return to Him in obedience and remain steadfast upon it. ﴿He will give you good enjoyment (mata' hasan) for a specified term.﴾ That is: He will benefit you in this world with provision, blessings, and good things. It was also said: it is the good life of the believer through his hope in Allah and his contentment with His decree, because the disbeliever may enjoy provision in this world. ﴿Until a specified term.﴾ That is, until death. ﴿And He will give every person of virtue his virtue.﴾ That is: He will give in the Hereafter every doer of deeds the reward of his deeds. The pronoun may refer back to Allah, the Exalted, or to "every person of virtue." ﴿But if you turn away...﴾ This is addressed to the people, and it is a imperfect verb from which one of the two taa's has been dropped. ﴿...the punishment of a great day.﴾ That is, the Day of Resurrection, or other than it, such as the Day of Badr.

Verily, they fold their breasts to hide from Him. ﴿Verily, they fold their breasts to hide from Him.﴾ It was said: when the disbelievers met the Messenger of God (ﷺ), they would turn their backs to him so that they would not see him, out of intense hatred and enmity. On this view, the pronoun in "منه" (from Him) refers to the Messenger of God (ﷺ). It was also said that this is an expression for what their breasts harbour of hatred and rancour. And it was said that it is an expression for their turning away, because whoever turns away from something folds back from it and deviates. On this view, the pronoun in "منه" refers to God Most High, meaning: they wish to hide from God Most High, so that neither His Messenger nor the believers would know what is in their hearts.

﴿Verily, when they cover themselves with their garments﴾, that is, they make them coverings and wrappings, out of aversion to hearing the Qur'an. The governing element of "حين" (when) is "يعلم" (He knows) in what they conceal and what they reveal. It was also said: the meaning is that they wish to hide when they cover themselves with their garments; on this view, one pauses at "منه" (from Him), and "يعلم" begins a new sentence.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 11, verse 6:

﴿And there is no creature on the earth but that its provision is upon Allah﴾. This is a promise and a true guarantee. If it is asked: how did He say "upon Allah" with the wording of obligation, when it is only a bounty (tafaddul), since nothing is obligatory upon Allah? The answer: He mentioned it in this way to emphasize the guarantee, for when He promised it, it became certain to occur without doubt, since He does not break His promise. ﴿And He knows its place of settlement and its place of storage﴾. The "mustawda'" (place of storage) is the loins of the father, and the "mustaqarr" (place of settlement) is the womb of the mother. It was also said: the "mustaqarr" is the place in this world, and the "mustawda'" is the grave.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 11, verse 7:

﴿And His Throne was upon the water﴾ is evidence that the Throne and the water existed before the creation of the heavens and the earth. ﴿That He may test you﴾ means: that He may test you with a test by which the proof is established against you, for He knew your deeds before He created you. "That He may test" is connected to the creation (of the heavens and the earth). ﴿It is nothing but evident magic﴾ may refer to the Qur'an, or to the claim of resurrection; they mean that it is false, like the falsehood of magic.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 11, verse 8:

﴿And if We defer the punishment from them﴾ It is possible that it means the punishment of this world or of the Hereafter. ﴿until a counted community﴾ i.e., until a limited time. ﴿they will surely say, "What is holding it back?"﴾ i.e., what is preventing this promised punishment? Their saying this is in the manner of denial and mockery.

﴿And if We let man taste mercy from Us, then withdraw it from him, indeed he is despairing and ungrateful﴾ [the verse]: a censure of the one who despairs at times of hardship, and of the one who boasts and becomes arrogant at times of blessings. Here "mercy" (al-rahmah) and "blessing" (al-na'ma') are intended to mean worldly good things. "Man" (al-insan) is general, meaning the species, and on this reading the exception (al-istithna', the excluding of a part from what precedes it) is continuous (muttasil). It is said that the intended "man" is the disbeliever, so the exception is disconnected (munqati').

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 11, verse 12:

﴿Perhaps you would leave out some of what is revealed to you﴾ etc.: The disbelievers used to propose to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he bring a treasure or that an angel come with him, and they used to mock the Qur'an. So Allah the Exalted said to him: Perhaps you are about to refrain from conveying to them some of what has been sent down to you, and it weighs heavily on you to convey it to them because of their mockery; or perhaps your breast is constricted because they say: "Why has a treasure not been sent down to him, or why has an angel not come with him?" The purpose of the verse is to console the Prophet (ﷺ) regarding their words, so that he conveys the message and does not care about them. He said ﴿ḍā'iq﴾ (constricted) and did not say ﴿ḍayyiq﴾, to indicate the breadth of his breast, peace be upon him, and the slightness of his constriction. ﴿Indeed, you are only a warner﴾: that is, there is nothing upon you except warning and conveying the message, and Allah is the Guardian (al-Wakil), who decides what He wills regarding their belief or their disbelief.

﴿Or do they say, "He has invented it"?﴾ Here "am" (أم) is disjunctive (munqati'a), meaning "bal" (بل, "rather"). The hamza and the pronoun in "iftarahu" (افتراه, "he invented it") refer to what is revealed to him. ﴿Say: "Then bring ten surahs like it"﴾ He challenged them first with ten surahs. When their inability became clear, He challenged them with a single surah, saying: "bring a surah like it" (فأتوا بسورة من مثله). The likeness required is in its eloquence and its sciences. ﴿invented﴾ is an attribute of "ten surahs," and this corresponds to their statement "he invented it." The likeness is not in invention. ﴿and call upon whomever you are able﴾ That is, seek help from whomever you wish. ﴿So if they do not respond to you﴾ Here there are two interpretations. The first: the address is from God to the Prophet ﷺ and the believers. That is, if the disbelievers do not respond to what you have called them to, namely opposing the Qur'an, then know that it is from God. This means: continue in your knowledge of that, or increase your certainty in it. The second: the address is from the Prophet ﷺ to the disbelievers. That is, if those whom you call upon besides God do not respond to any opposition, and all of you are unable to do it, then know that it is from God. This second interpretation is stronger than the first because of His saying: ﴿Will you then submit?﴾ The meaning of "bi-'ilm Allah" (بعلم الله) is "with His permission," or "with what none knows but God of the unseen." His saying ﴿Will you then submit?﴾ is phrased as a question, but its meaning is an invitation to Islam and an obligation upon the disbelievers to submit, since He has stated the proof for the truth of Islam, namely their inability to produce the like of the Qur'an.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 11, verses 15–16:

﴿Whoever desires the life of this world and its adornment﴾ etc.: It was revealed concerning the disbelievers who desire this world and do not desire the Hereafter, since they do not believe in it. It has also been said that it was revealed concerning the hypocrites (ahl al-riya') among the believers, who intend by their deeds the world, according to what has been reported in the hadith concerning the reciter (of the Qur'an), the one who spends (in charity), and the fighter in jihad, who wanted to be called such: "They are the first whom the Fire will be kindled for." The first view is more preponderant, because the mention of the disbelievers who contradict the Qur'an came before, and it is those who are intended by this verse. ﴿We will pay them their deeds therein﴾: We will pay them the rewards of their deeds with what they are envied for therein, namely health and provision. The pronoun in "therein" refers to the world, and the prepositional phrase is connected either to the words "We will pay" or to "their deeds." ﴿And what they did therein is nullified﴾: The pronoun in "therein" here refers to the Hereafter if the prepositional phrase is connected to "nullified," and it refers to the world if it is connected to "they did."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 11, verse 17:

﴿Is he who is upon clear evidence from his Lord﴾. The intended meaning of "he who is upon clear evidence from his Lord" is the Prophet (ﷺ) and the believers, as indicated by His words that follow: ﴿They believe in it﴾. The meaning of "bayyinah" (clear evidence) is rational proof and manifest matter. ﴿And a witness from Him recites it﴾. The pronoun in "yatluhu" (recites it) refers to the proof, which is the bayyinah, and to the one who is upon clear evidence from his Lord. The pronoun in "minhu" (from Him) refers to the Lord, exalted is He. "Yatluhu" here means "yattabi'uhu" (follows it). The "witness" is intended to refer to the Qur'an, so the meaning is: that proof is followed by a witness from Allah, which is the Qur'an, so its clarity increases and its indication becomes greater. It has also been said that the witness mentioned here is 'Ali ibn Abi Talib. ﴿And before it was the Book of Musa﴾, meaning: and before that witnessing book was the Book of Musa, which is also another earlier proof. It has been said that there are many opinions regarding the meaning of this verse, and the most preferred of them is what we have mentioned. ﴿And of the factions﴾ [al-Ra'd: 36], meaning: from the people of Makkah.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 11, verses 18–23:

﴿And the witnesses will say﴾: "al-ashhad" is the plural of "shahid," like "ashab" (companions). It may come from shahada (testimony), in which case it refers to the angels and the prophets; or it may come from shuhud in the sense of presence, in which case it refers to everyone who was present at the gathering place. ﴿And they seek to make it crooked﴾: that is, they seek its crookedness or describe it as crooked. ﴿They could not escape﴾: that is, they could not slip away. ﴿Their punishment will be doubled﴾: this is a report of the intensification of their punishment, and it is not a description of the friends of God. ﴿They were not able to hear﴾ (the verse): "ma" here is a negation and the pronoun refers to the disbelievers. The meaning is that God described them as those who neither hear nor see, like their saying: ﴿God has set a seal upon their hearts﴾ [al-Baqarah: 7] (the verse). It has been said otherwise, but that is far-fetched. ﴿Undoubtedly﴾ (la jarama): that is, there is no doubt and no question about it. ﴿And they humbled themselves﴾: that is, they submitted humbly; it has also been said that it means they turned back in repentance (anabu).

The parable of the two groups (﴿مَثَلُ ٱلْفَرِيقَيْنِ﴾), meaning the believers and the disbelievers, is ﴿like the blind and the deaf, and the seeing and the hearing﴾. He likened the disbelievers to the blind and the deaf, and likened the believers to the seeing and the hearing. So on this reading it is a parable of the believers with two examples and a parable of the disbelievers with two examples. It was also said: the intended construction is "like the blind and the deaf, and the seeing and the hearing," so the waw (و) is for coordinating the attributes. On this reading it is a parable of the believers with one example, namely one who combines hearing and sight, and a parable of the disbelievers with one example, namely one who combines blindness and deafness.

"the painful day": he described the day as painful metaphorically, because pain occurs in it. ﴿أَرَاذِلُنَا﴾ is the plural of "arrdhal", and they are the lowest of people. They described them thus because of their poverty, out of ignorance and in the belief that nobility lies in wealth and status. The matter is not as they believed; rather, the believers were nobler than them in their state of poverty and obscurity in this world. It was also said that they were weavers and cuppers. Ibn 'Atiyya chose that they meant they were lowly in their actions, based on Nuh's words: ﴿And I have no knowledge of what they used to do﴾.

﴿بَادِيَ ٱلرَّأْيِ﴾: that is, the first of opinion, without reflection or deliberation. "Badi" is in the accusative of time (ẓarf), its original sense being the time when their first opinion arose. The governing word for it is "they followed you", according to the most correct opinions. The meaning is: the lowly ones followed you without reflection or deliberation. It was also said that it is an attribute of "a human like us", meaning: not firm in opinion.

﴿وَمَا نَرَىٰ لَكُمْ عَلَيْنَا مِن فَضْلٍ﴾: that is, any merit or nobility. The address is to Nuh, peace be upon him, and those with him.

﴿Upon a clear proof from my Lord﴾: that is, upon a demonstrative proof and a manifest matter. The same applies to the stories of Salih and Shu'ayb.

﴿And has given me mercy from Him﴾: meaning prophethood.

﴿But it has been made obscure to you﴾: that is, it has been hidden from you. The subject (fa'il) of "made obscure," according to this reading, is "the proof" or "the mercy."

﴿وَقَالَ ٱرْكَبُواْ فِيهَا﴾ "And he said, 'Embark therein.'" The pronoun in "qala" (he said) refers to Nuh, and the address is to those who were with him. The pronoun in "fiha" (therein) refers to the ship. It is related that they boarded it on the first day of Rajab, and that it came to rest on al-Judi on the day of 'Ashura'. ﴿بِسْمِ ٱللَّهِ مَجْريٰهَا وَمُرْسَٰهَا﴾ "In the name of Allah is its sailing and its anchoring." The derivation of "majriha" is from "jary" (running), and the derivation of "mursaha" is from "irsa'" (anchoring), which means firmness. It may also be derived from the ship's standing still. Both words may be adverbs of time or place, or verbal nouns. The i'rab (grammatical analysis) allows two possibilities:

The first: the name of Allah occupies the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "irkabu" (embark). The meaning is: "Embark seeking blessing in the name of Allah," or "saying 'In the name of Allah.'" On this reading, "majriha" and "mursaha" are adverbs of time, meaning the time of its running and its anchoring, or adverbs of place. The governing element is the sense of a verb contained in "bismillah" in the position of a predicate. "Bismillah" is connected with what precedes it, and the whole is one utterance.

The second: they form two separate utterances. One stops at "irkabu fiha" (embark therein), "bismillah" occupies the position of a predicate, and "majriha wa mursaha" is a subject in the sense of a verbal noun, meaning "its running and its anchoring." On this reading, "bismillah" is a new, independent clause not connected with what precedes it, but it is part of Nuh's speech, as it is related that when Nuh wished the ship to run he said "bismillah," and it ran, and when he wished it to stop he said "bismillah," and it stopped.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 11, verses 44–48:

﴿O earth, swallow your water﴾: an expression for the ground drying of water. ﴿And O sky, withhold﴾: i.e., hold back from rain. It is narrated that it had rained from every place on the earth. ﴿The water subsided﴾: i.e., decreased. ﴿And the matter was decided﴾: i.e., was completed and finished. ﴿And it came to rest upon al-Judi﴾: i.e., the ship settled upon al-Judi, which is a mountain in Mosul. ﴿And it was said, "Away with the wrongdoing people!"﴾: i.e., destruction, and it is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar). ﴿And Noah called to his Lord﴾: this call may have been before the drowning, in which case the conjunction is without sequence (ordering), or it may have been after it. ﴿So he said, "My Lord, indeed my son is of my family"﴾: i.e., and You had promised me that You would save my family. ﴿He said, "O Noah, indeed he is not of your family"﴾: i.e., he is not of your family whose salvation You had promised you, because he was a disbeliever, and because of His saying: "And Noah called his son." ﴿Indeed, he is [one whose] work is other than righteous﴾: On the reading of the majority, there are three interpretations. The first: the pronoun in "indeed he" refers to Noah's request for his son's salvation. The second: the pronoun refers to Noah's son, and an element has been omitted from the speech, its implied meaning being: "indeed he is one possessing unrighteous work." The third: the pronoun refers to Noah's son, and "work" is a masdar used as a description for emphasis, like your saying "a man of fasting" (sawm). Al-Kisa'i read "ʿamila" as a past-tense verb with "ghayra ṣāliḥin" in the accusative; on this reading the pronoun refers to Noah's son without any difficulty. ﴿So do not ask Me about that of which you have no knowledge﴾: i.e., do not ask Me for a matter about which you do not know whether it is right or wrong, until you have understood its reality. If it is said: why did he call his call a "question" when there is no question in it? The answer is that it contained a question even though it was not stated explicitly. ﴿Indeed, I advise you, lest you be among the ignorant﴾: "lest" (an) is in the position of an object of purpose; the meaning is: I advise you out of dislike that you would be among the ignorant. There is in this no description of him as ignorant; rather it contains gentleness and honour. ﴿Descend with peace from Us﴾: i.e., descend from the ship in safety. ﴿And [upon] nations [descending] from those with you﴾: i.e., from those who are with you in the ship. Al-Zamakhshari preferred that the meaning be "from the descendants of those with you," meaning the believers until the Day of Resurrection; on this reading "min" is for the beginning of the extent (ibtida' al-ghaya), and the implied sense is "upon nations originating from those with you." On the first reading, "min" is for specifying the kind (bayan al-jins). ﴿And [other] nations We will provide for; then a painful punishment will touch them from Us﴾: i.e., We will grant them enjoyment of the worldly life, and they are the disbelievers, until the Day of Resurrection.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 11, verse 57–58:

﴿So if you turn away, then I have already conveyed to you﴾ The original form of "tawallaw" here is "tatawallaw," because it is an imperfect verb from which the taa' of the present tense has been dropped. If it is asked: how did the conveying come as the answer to the condition, when the conveying was before the turning away? The answer is: the meaning is, "If you turn away, then there is no blame upon me, because I have indeed conveyed to you the message of my Lord." ﴿And you will not harm Him at all﴾ meaning, you will not diminish Him in anything; that is, if He destroys you and substitutes others in your place. ﴿And when Our command came﴾ If it is asked: why does it say here, and in the story of Shu'ayb, "wa-lamma" (and when) with the waw, but in the story of Salih and Lut it says "fa-lamma" (so when) with the fa'? The answer, according to what al-Zamakhshari said, is that in the story of Salih and Lut this came after the threat, so the fa' was used, which denotes causation, as you say, "I promised him, so when the appointment came..." In contrast with the story of Hud and Shu'ayb, where nothing of that sort preceded it in those two, so the conjunction used was the waw. ﴿And We saved them from a severe punishment﴾ It may be that he intends by it the punishment of the Hereafter, and for that reason he joined it to the first salvation, which he intended as salvation from the wind. It may also be that he intends by the second as well the wind, and he repeated it to inform that it is a severe punishment and to enumerate the blessing of their salvation.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 11, verses 59–60:

﴿And they disobeyed His messengers.﴾ Regarding "the messengers" here, there are two interpretations. The first: whoever disobeys one messenger is obligated to disobey all of them, since they are all in agreement on faith in God and on His unity. Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 11, verses 77–83:

﴿And when Our messengers came to Lut, he was distressed on their account and felt helpless concerning them﴾. "The messengers" (al-rusul) are the angels. The meaning of "sa'a bihim" is that he was afflicted by evil (su'), and he was distressed (shaja) when he thought they were among the children of Adam and feared for them from his people. ﴿A day of distress﴾, that is, severe. ﴿And his people came rushing to him﴾, that is, hastening. Lut's wife had informed them of the arrival of the guests at his house, so they hurried to do their vile deed with them. ﴿And before this they used to commit evil deeds﴾, that is, their custom was to commit abominations with males. ﴿He said: "O my people, these are my daughters"﴾. The meaning is: marry them. He only said that to protect his guests with his daughters. It is also said that the name of one daughter was Ria, and the other Ghawth, and that the name of his wife who was destroyed was Wahila, and the name of Noah's wife was Waqila. ﴿They said: "You know that we have no claim on your daughters"﴾, that is, we have no desire for them. ﴿And you certainly know what we want﴾, meaning intercourse with males. ﴿He said: "If only I had power against you"﴾: the answer to "law" is omitted, its estimated meaning being: "If I had the ability to repel you, I would have done it." It may also be that "law" expresses wishing. ﴿Or that I could take refuge in a strong support﴾. The meaning of "a'wi" is "I seek refuge." By "a strong support" is meant what one takes refuge in, such as a clan and helpers who protect him from his people. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to say: "May Allah have mercy on my brother Lut; he used to take refuge in a strong support," meaning in Allah and the angels. ﴿They said: "O Lut, we are messengers of your Lord"﴾. The pronoun in "qalu" refers to the angels, and the pronoun in "lan yasilu" refers to the people of Lut, for Allah had then blinded their eyes. ﴿So travel with your family by night﴾, that is, take them out at night, for the punishment will descend upon the people of these cities. It is recited as "fa-asri" with the alif both connected and cut, and both are dialects: it is said "sara" and "asra." ﴿In a portion of the night﴾, that is, a part of it. ﴿And let none of you look back﴾. They were forbidden to look back, lest their hearts be broken over their town. It is also said that "yaltafit" means "yaltawi" (turn aside). ﴿Except your wife﴾. It is read with both the accusative and the nominative. The accusative makes it an exception from "so travel with your family," which implies that he did not take her out with his family. The nominative makes it a substitute for "none of you," and it is related on this reading that he took her out with him, and that she looked back and said: "O my people!" and a stone struck her and killed her. ﴿Indeed, their appointed time is the morning﴾, that is, the time of their punishment is the morning. ﴿Is not the morning near?﴾ It is mentioned that when they said, "Their appointed time is the morning," Lut said to them: "Would that they were punished now." They said to him: "Is not the morning near?" ﴿We made its highest part its lowest﴾. The pronoun refers to the cities. It is related that Gabriel put his wing beneath the cities of the people of Lut, uprooted them, and lifted them until the people of heaven heard the crowing of roosters and the barking of dogs, and then he overturned them. ﴿And We rained upon them stones﴾, that is, upon the cities, meaning their inhabitants. It is related that whoever among them was outside the cities was struck by stones from heaven, and as for those who were within the cities, they perished when they were overturned. ﴿Of baked clay﴾. It is said the meaning is of water and clay, and it was of baked brick. It is also said it is from "sajjalahu" meaning "he sent it." It is also said that it is a non-Arabic word. ﴿Layered, one upon another﴾, that is, some of it piled upon the rest. ﴿Marked by your Lord﴾. The meaning is: marked with a sign. It is related that it had white and red coloring, and it is said that each stone bore the name of its target. ﴿And it is not far from the wrongdoers﴾. The pronoun refers to the stones, and "the wrongdoers" means the disbelievers of Quraysh. This is a warning to them: the stoning is not far from them because of their disbelief. It is also said the pronoun refers to the cities, so the meaning is: they are not far from them, so will they not take heed from them, as in His saying: ﴿And they have certainly passed by the town on which a rain of evil was rained﴾ [al-Furqan: 40]. It is also said that "the wrongdoers" is general in meaning.

The meaning is: marry them. He only said that to protect his guests with his daughters. It is also said that the name of one daughter was Ria, and the other Ghawth, and that the name of his wife who was destroyed was Wahila, and the name of Noah's wife was Waqila. ﴿They said: "You know that we have no claim on your daughters"﴾, that is, we have no desire for them. ﴿And you certainly know what we want﴾, meaning intercourse with males. ﴿He said: "If only I had power against you"﴾: the answer to "law" is omitted, its estimated meaning being: "If I had the ability to repel you, I would have done it." It is said the meaning is of water and clay, and it was of baked brick. It is also said it is from "sajjalahu" meaning "he sent it." Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 11, verses 84–88:

﴿Indeed, I see you in prosperity﴾, meaning cheap prices and abundant provision, ﴿and indeed I fear for you the punishment of an all-encompassing day﴾, the Day of Resurrection, or the day of their punishment in this world.

﴿What remains from Allah [i.e., His lawful provision] is better for you﴾, meaning what Allah has left for you of His provision and blessings.

﴿Does your prayer command you﴾, the prayer (al-salah) being the well-known act of worship, and attributing the command to it is a metaphor, like His saying: ﴿Indeed, the prayer forbids immorality and wrongdoing﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 45]. The meaning is: does your prayer command you that we abandon the worship of idols? The disbelievers said this in a mocking manner.

﴿Or that we do with our wealth what we wish﴾, meaning what they were accustomed to of cheating in measure and weight. The phrase "and that we do" is coordinated (ma'tuf) with "that we abandon".

﴿Indeed, you are the forbearing, the rightly guided﴾. It has been said: they said this in a manner of sarcasm and mockery. It has also been said: the meaning is "forbearing, rightly guided" regarding yourself.

﴿And He has provided me from Himself with good provision﴾, meaning free from the corruption you have introduced into your wealth. The answer to "ara'aytum" (tell me) is omitted, indicated by the meaning, and its estimated sense is: "Tell me, if I am upon clear evidence from my Lord, would it be proper for me to abandon conveying His message?"

﴿And I do not intend to oppose you by doing what I forbid you from.﴾ It is said: "Khalafani fulan ila kadha" when a person intends something while you turn away from it, and "khalafani 'anhu" when he turns away from it while you intend it.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 11, verses 89–92:

﴿And O my people, let not my opposition (shiqaq) bring upon you the like of what befell the people of Noah﴾. That is: let not my enmity lead you to earn (yakṣibanna) the punishment like that of the earlier nations. Shiqaqi is the subject (fa'il), and an yuṣība-kum is the object (maf'ul).

﴿And the people of Lot are not far from you﴾. That is, in time, for they were the nearest of the destroyed nations to them. It is also possible that "far" is meant in terms of place.

﴿We do not understand (ma naqqahu)﴾, that is, we do not comprehend.

﴿And indeed we see you among us as weak﴾. That is, weak in victory and power. It was also said: frail of body. And it was said: blind.

﴿Were it not for your clan (rahṭuka), we would have stoned you﴾. Rahṭ means kinsfolk. Stoning is with stones, or with reviling.

﴿Is my clan more esteemed by you than God?﴾ This is a rebuke to them. If it is asked: their speech was about him and his clan, that they were the honored ones and not he; so how does his answer correspond to their speech? The answer is that their slighting of him, who was the Messenger of God, was a slighting of God; therefore he said: "Is my clan more esteemed by you than God?"

﴿And you have taken Him behind your backs (waraa'akum ẓihriyyan)﴾. The pronoun in "ittakhadhtumūhu" refers to God Most High, or to His religion and command. And "ẓihrī" is that which is cast behind the back and not regarded; it is a relative adjective derived from "ẓahr" (back) with a change in its nisba form.

﴿And O my people, let not my opposition (shiqaq) bring upon you the like of what befell the people of Noah﴾. That is: let not my enmity lead you to earn (yakṣibanna) the punishment like that of the earlier nations. Shiqaqi is the subject (fa'il), and an yuṣība-kum is the object (maf'ul).

﴿And the people of Lot are not far from you﴾. That is, in time, for they were the nearest of the destroyed nations to them. It is also possible that "far" is meant in terms of place.

﴿We do not understand (ma naqqahu)﴾, that is, we do not comprehend.

﴿And indeed we see you among us as weak﴾. That is, weak in victory and power. It was also said: frail of body. And it was said: blind.

﴿Were it not for your clan (rahṭuka), we would have stoned you﴾. Rahṭ means kinsfolk. Stoning is with stones, or with reviling.

﴿Is my clan more esteemed by you than God?﴾ This is a rebuke to them. If it is asked: their speech was about him and his clan, that they were the honored ones and not he; so how does his answer correspond to their speech? The answer is that their slighting of him, who was the Messenger of God, was a slighting of God; therefore he said: "Is my clan more esteemed by you than God?"

﴿And you have taken Him behind your backs (waraa'akum ẓihriyyan)﴾. The pronoun in "ittakhadhtumūhu" refers to God Most High, or to His religion and command. And "ẓihrī" is that which is cast behind the back and not regarded; it is a relative adjective derived from "ẓahr" (back) with a change in its nisba form.

"Work according to your position" (Qur'an 11:93): a threat. Its meaning, "your position," refers to your established power in the world and your honour in it. "Whoever will be visited by a punishment that disgraces him" refers to the punishment of this world and the Hereafter. "And watch" (Qur'an 11:93): a threat.

﴿And We certainly sent Moses with Our signs﴾, that is, with the miracles, ﴿and a clear authority﴾, that is, a manifest proof. ﴿He will lead his people﴾, that is, he will go ahead of them into the Fire, just as they used to follow him in this world into misguidance and disbelief. ﴿So he will bring them down to the Fire﴾. The word "al-wurud" (coming down to, arriving at) here means entering. It is expressed in the past tense to indicate that it is certain to occur. ﴿And on the Day of Resurrection﴾ is coordinated (ʿatf, coordination) with "in this [world]", for what is meant by it is in this world. ﴿Wretched is the gift that is given﴾, that is, the gift that is bestowed. ﴿Standing and cut down﴾, that is, remaining and obliterated. ﴿So their gods availed them not﴾ is evidence for monotheism and the negation of partners. ﴿Ruin﴾, that is, loss. ﴿That is a Day on which mankind will be gathered﴾, that is, they will be assembled on it for reckoning, reward, and punishment. He expressed it with the passive participle (ism al-maful, the noun of the one acted upon) rather than the verb in order to indicate that gathering is established for that day, because the word "majmuʿ" (gathered) is more eloquent than the word "yajmaʿ" (he gathers). ﴿And it is a Day witnessed﴾, that is, the first and the last will attend it.

﴿On the day it comes﴾. The element governing the adverbial phrase (al-zarf) is either ﴿لا تكلم﴾ (lā tukallim, "no one shall speak") or an implied verb (fi'l mudmar). The subject of ﴿يأت﴾ (ya'ti, "it comes") is a pronoun referring back to "a Day witnessed" (yawm mashhūd). Al-Zamakhshari said that it refers to God, the Exalted, as in His saying: ﴿Or your Lord comes﴾ [al-An'am: 158]. This is supported by the pronoun's return to Him in His words: ﴿by His permission﴾. ﴿Among them are the wretched and the blessed﴾. The pronoun refers to the people of the standing place (ahl al-mawqif), which is indicated by His words: "no soul shall speak". ﴿Groaning and sighing﴾. Al-zafir is the expelling of breath, and al-shahīq is its drawing back. It was also said: al-zafir is the sound of the grieving person, and al-shahīq is the sound of the weeping person. It was also said: al-zafir comes from the throat, and al-shahīq from the chest. ﴿Abiding therein for as long as the heavens and the earth endure﴾. There are two interpretations. The first is that it refers to the heavens and earth of the Hereafter, which endure forever. The second is that it is an expression for perpetuity, like the Arabs' saying: "no star has risen and no dove has mourned," and similar expressions intended to convey permanence. ﴿Except what your Lord wills﴾. There are three opinions concerning this exception. It was said that it is a matter of courtesy toward God, like your saying "if God wills," even though the matter is certain. It was said that it refers to the period of the sinners' exit from the Fire, and that "those who are wretched" on this view includes both disbelievers and sinners. It was said that it refers to the duration of their existence in this world and in the barzakh. As for the exception concerning the people of Paradise, the first and third opinions are valid there, but not the second. ﴿Unending﴾, meaning not cut off.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 11, verses 109–111:

﴿So do not be in doubt concerning what these worship﴾. Al-miriyah (doubt, uncertainty). The reference is to the idol-worshippers, meaning: do not doubt the corruption of the religion of these people. ﴿They worship only as their fathers worshipped before⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿—﻿﻿﻿—they follow their fathers by blind imitation (taqlid) without any proof﴾. ﴿And indeed, We will give them their full share﴾, meaning of the punishment. ﴿A word that preceded﴾, meaning: the decree (al-qadr). That is because Allah decreed that He would judge between them on the Day of Resurrection, and would not judge between them in this world. ﴿And indeed, all of them﴾: it has been read with a shaddah on inna and with its shaddah removed, and governing its action as the heavy (thaqilah) form; the tanwin on kull is a substitute for the genitive noun that was omitted, meaning "all of them." The lam in la-lamma is the preparatory lam for an oath, and ma is extra (za'idah), and la-yuwaffiyannahum is the predicate of inna. It has also been read as lamma with shaddah, on the basis that inna is negative (nafiyah), and lamma means illa (except). ﴿Your Lord will surely repay them in full for their deeds﴾, meaning: the recompense of their deeds.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 11, verses 112–114:

﴿And do not incline toward those who have wronged﴾. He means: the disbelievers. It was also said: they are the oppressive rulers and others. ﴿Then you will not be helped﴾: this is a new sentence, not conjoined (to what precedes). He said "then" (thumma) only to indicate the remoteness of help. ﴿And establish prayer﴾, etc.: it means the obligatory prayers. The first extremity (ṭaraf) is the dawn prayer, and the second extremity is the noon and afternoon prayers, and "zulaf" from the night refers to the sunset and night prayers. ﴿Indeed, good deeds remove bad deeds﴾: its wording is general, and the commentators (ahl al-ta'wil) specified it, saying that the good deeds are the five daily prayers. It is possible that this is by way of example. It is narrated that a man kissed a woman and then regretted it, so he mentioned that to the Prophet (ﷺ) and prayed with him the prayer. Then the verse was revealed, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Where is the questioner?" He said: "Here I am." He said: "You have been forgiven." The man said: "Is it for me specifically, or for the Muslims generally?" He said: "Rather, for the Muslims generally." According to this, the verse is Medinan. It was also said: the verse was before that, and the Prophet (ﷺ) mentioned it to the man as evidence, so according to this the verse is Meccan, like the rest of the surah. According to the majority, good deeds remove only minor sins when major sins are avoided. ﴿That﴾ refers to the prayers, or to everything mentioned before of admonition, promise and warning.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 11, verses 112–114:

﴿And do not incline toward those who have wronged﴾. He means: the disbelievers. It was also said: they are the oppressive rulers and others. ﴿Then you will not be helped﴾: this is a new sentence, not conjoined (to what precedes). He said "then" (thumma) only to indicate the remoteness of help. ﴿And establish prayer﴾, etc.: it means the obligatory prayers. The first extremity (ṭaraf) is the dawn prayer, and the second extremity is the noon and afternoon prayers, and "zulaf" from the night refers to the sunset and night prayers. ﴿Indeed, good deeds remove bad deeds﴾: its wording is general, and the commentators (ahl al-ta'wil) specified it, saying that the good deeds are the five daily prayers. It is possible that this is by way of example. It is narrated that a man kissed a woman and then regretted it, so he mentioned that to the Prophet (ﷺ) and prayed with him the prayer. Then the verse was revealed, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Where is the questioner?" He said: "Here I am." He said: "You have been forgiven." The man said: "Is it for me specifically, or for the Muslims generally?" He said: "Rather, for the Muslims generally." According to this, the verse is Medinan. It was also said: the verse was before that, and the Prophet (ﷺ) mentioned it to the man as evidence, so according to this the verse is Meccan, like the rest of the surah. According to the majority, good deeds remove only minor sins when major sins are avoided. ﴿That﴾ refers to the prayers, or to everything mentioned before of admonition, promise and warning.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 11, verse 116:

﴿Why then were there not﴾ (talḥīḍ, meaning "why not" or "would that there were") ﴿among the generations before you people of virtue (ulū baqiyyah)﴾, i.e., people of goodness and religion remaining among them, apart from others, ﴿except a few of those whom We saved from among them﴾. This is an exceptive phrase (istithnā' munqaṭi'), its meaning being: "But a few of those generations whom We saved used to forbid corruption on the earth." It is also said that it is a connected exception (istithnā' muttaṣil), since the statement preceding it has the force of negation, as if he said: "There was not among them anyone who forbade corruption on the earth, except a few," and the usual construction for such a substitute (badal) is the nominative, though the accusative is also permissible. ﴿Those who did wrong﴾ means those who did not forbid corruption on the earth.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 11, verse 117–122:

﴿بِظُلْمٍ﴾ This prepositional phrase (majrur) here occupies the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to ﴿رَبُّكَ﴾ (your Lord). The meaning is that He does not destroy the people of the towns while they are wrongdoers, exalted is Allah above that. ﴿وَلَوْ شَآءَ رَبُّكَ لَجَعَلَ ٱلنَّاسَ أُمَّةً وَاحِدَةً﴾ (And if your Lord had willed, He would have made mankind one community.) That is, a community of believers, with no disagreement among them regarding faith. ﴿وَلاَ يَزَالُونَ مُخْتَلِفِينَ﴾ (But they will continue to differ.) That is, in religions, creeds (milal) and legal schools (madhahib). ﴿وَلِذٰلِكَ خَلَقَهُمْ﴾ (And for that He created them.) It has been said: the reference (ishara) is to the difference; it has been said: to mercy; and it has been said: to both of them. ﴿وَكُـلاًّ نَّقُصُّ﴾ (And each [of] We relate to you.) The word ﴿كلاً﴾ is in the accusative governed by ﴿نقص﴾ (We relate), and ﴿ما﴾ is a substitute (badal) for ﴿كلاً﴾. ﴿وَجَآءَكَ فِي هَـٰذِهِ ٱلْحَقُّ﴾ (And there has come to you in this the truth.) The reference (ishara) is to the surah. ﴿ٱعْمَلُواْ... وَٱنْتَظِرُوۤاْ﴾ (Act... and wait.) This is a threat to them and an establishment of proof (iqamat hujja) against them.
